lesson_title: The Missing Corner: Completing the Square
hook_text: A patio with one empty corner. Fill it, and you can solve any quadratic alive.
clip_script: Your family is paving a square patio, x metres by x metres. Then a delivery arrives — enough pavers for eight x more square metres — and the plan says the patio must end up a perfect square again. So you split the extra into two strips, four metres wide: one down the side, one along the bottom. Step back. It's an L-shape. Almost a big square of side x plus four — except one corner is empty. Measure it: exactly four by four. Sixteen square metres. Drop sixteen in and the patio is perfect. That gap is completing the square. Halve the middle number — eight becomes four. Square it — four becomes sixteen. That's the missing corner, every single time. And in an equation, adding sixteen to one side means adding sixteen to the other, or the equals sign breaks. So x squared plus eight x equals minus three becomes x plus four, all squared, equals thirteen. Last move, where the mark hides: a square of thirteen has TWO possible sides — root thirteen and minus root thirteen. Plus or minus, always. Two answers: minus four plus root thirteen, and minus four minus root thirteen.
visual_style: Top-down view of a backyard build: grey pavers forming a square, a fresh pallet splitting into two long strips, an L-shape with one glowing empty corner, then a single square tile dropping in as the whole patio flashes complete.
mood: Hands-on and satisfying, like watching a build come together.
pacing: Calm while the patio grows, a held beat on the empty corner, quick and clean through the algebra.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and crack the quadratics that refuse to factorise.
